title: Trump pardoned his daughter's father-in-law Charles Kushner, then made him ambassador to France

business_entity.name: Kushner Companies
business_entity.family_stake: Charles Kushner founded Kushner Companies, a New Jersey-based real estate firm, in 1985 and became its chairman; AP describes him as the firm's founder. His son Jared Kushner is married to Ivanka Trump. Kushner's current ownership share in the firm is not public.

government_nexus.action: Trump's full and unconditional pardon of Charles Kushner on December 23, 2020, followed by Trump's 2025 nomination of Kushner as U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco, which the Senate confirmed 51-45 on May 19, 2025.
government_nexus.note: The link is a family tie, not a business deal: Trump used two presidential powers, clemency and appointment, for the same person, the father of his son-in-law Jared Kushner. No official act benefiting Kushner Companies has been reported. A pardon restores legal standing but does not erase the underlying conduct from public scrutiny, and the family relationship raises a nepotism concern separate from whether the pardon itself was proper.

status: Serving as U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco; the Senate confirmed him 51-45 on May 19, 2025, and he was sworn in on July 11, 2025.
what_changed: Charles Kushner, father of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, pleaded guilty in 2004 to 18 felony counts including tax evasion, making illegal campaign contributions, and witness retaliation -- **the retaliation count stemmed from Kushner hiring a prostitute to seduce his brother-in-law (a cooperating witness against him) and sending a video of the encounter to his own sister**. Trump pardoned Kushner in December 2020, during his first term's final weeks. In 2025, Trump nominated Kushner to serve as U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Kushner acknowledged the underlying conduct as a 'serious mistake.' On May 19, 2025, the Senate confirmed Kushner by a vote of 51-45, with Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) breaking with nearly all Democratic colleagues to vote in favor, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) voting against confirmation despite being a Republican.

financial_stake.summary: No money is reported to have flowed to a family business from the pardon or the appointment. The stake is the post itself and the family tie: Kushner is a wealthy real estate developer who founded Kushner Companies and has donated significant amounts to Trump's campaigns, and the Paris embassy is a post usually given to a major donor or close ally of the president.
financial_stake.caveat: There are no dollar figures to weigh here. Trump praised Kushner as "a tremendous business leader, philanthropist and dealmaker" when he named him, and his 2020 pardon cited Kushner's record of "reform" and "charity". Kushner told senators "I made a very, very, very serious mistake" and argued his past made him "more qualified to do this job." Supporters can also argue the conduct is two decades old, that he served his sentence, that a pardon is meant to allow full reintegration including public service, and that choosing ambassadors is a legitimate presidential prerogative.

legal_context: Both acts rest on constitutional presidential powers: the pardon on the Pardon Clause (U.S. Const. art. II, sec. 2, cl. 1) and the ambassadorship on the Appointments Clause (art. II, sec. 2, cl. 2), which the Senate exercised by confirming him. Neither has been found unlawful, and no legal challenge has been reported. This is lawful-but-concerning conduct: the concern is pairing a pardon with a prestigious post for a member of the president's extended family whose crimes included retaliating against a federal witness.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the underlying conviction, the 2020 pardon, the nomination, the hearing testimony and the confirmation vote breakdown are all well-documented public record, corroborated across The Hill, Reuters and AP reporting. What is disputed is the characterization: critics see the pardon-then-appointment sequence as a reward for family ties, while Trump and Senate supporters treat it as a legitimate use of two presidential powers for a rehabilitated businessman. There is no public figure for any financial benefit, and no reporting ties the appointment to a Kushner Companies business interest.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this database documents of Trump using both pardon power and appointment power to reward personal loyalty and family connections, sometimes in combination (a pardon followed by a prestigious appointment for the same individual), rather than as fully independent exercises of each power.

title: Kushner's Affinity Partners won a free Belgrade lease and a fast-track law for a $500M Trump Tower, then quit as Serbian officials were charged

business_entity.name: Affinity Partners
business_entity.family_stake: Jared Kushner founded and leads Affinity Partners (Semafor; BIRN describes it as owned by him), and the deal ran through Kushner-linked Affinity Global Development, which signed the 99-year lease (AP). The New York Times, as relayed by Vreme, reported that the Trump Organization, managed by Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr., was also involved because the hotel would carry the Trump brand; no licensing terms have been reported.

government_nexus.action: Serbia's government agreed to give the Kushner-linked company a 99-year lease on the former Yugoslav army headquarters site, its parliament passed a November 2025 special law fast-tracking the project and annulling the site's heritage status, and officials stripped the site's cultural-monument protection in a step prosecutors say rested on a forged document.

also_officials.name: Nikola Selaković
also_officials.role: Minister of Culture of Serbia (charged December 2025; denies the charges)

government_nexus.note: Vučić personally backed the project and said it would be good for Serbia's relations with the United States, at a time when the Trump administration had imposed 35% tariffs on Serbian imports and sanctioned Serbia's Russian-controlled oil supplier; a ruling-party lawmaker said he hoped it would improve ties with the Trump administration. The terms (a lease the Times says carried no costs, plus fast-track legislation) went to a firm owned by the sitting president's son-in-law. No source reports a confirmed exchange with any U.S. policy decision, and Kushner is not accused of the forgery.

status: Project withdrawn December 15, 2025. Selaković and the three other officials went on trial in Belgrade's Higher Court in February 2026 and deny the charges; hearings continued through September 2026 with no verdict.
date_of_action: 2025-11 (Serbia fast-tracks Trump Tower Belgrade project) through 2025-12-15 (prosecutors file forgery and abuse-of-office charges against officials, Kushner firm withdraws)
what_changed: Affinity Partners, the investment firm Jared Kushner founded after leaving his White House post, partnered with Dubai billionaire Mohamed Alabbar to develop a roughly $500 million Trump Tower hotel and apartment complex in Belgrade, Serbia, on the site of the former Yugoslav army headquarters -- a building bombed by NATO in 1999 and protected as a cultural monument. The Serbian government, led by President Aleksandar Vučić, agreed to grant Affinity Partners a 99-year lease to the site at no cost and, in November 2025, passed legislation to fast-track the project's approval; Vučić's government publicly framed the deal as a way to strengthen ties with the Trump administration at a time when the U.S. had imposed 35% tariffs on Serbian imports and sanctioned NIS, Serbia's Russian-controlled oil monopoly. Serbian organized-crime prosecutors alleged the government's decision removing the site's historic-monument protection rested on a falsified proposal from Serbia's Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, drafted without the Institute's conservation experts; **on December 15, 2025 prosecutors filed an indictment proposal charging Serbian Culture Minister Nikola Selaković -- a close Vučić ally -- along with three other officials with abuse of office and document falsification for their roles in stripping that protection to clear the way for the project**. Affinity Partners announced its withdrawal on December 15, 2025, the day the charges were filed and after a year of public protests against the project, stating that 'out of respect for the people of Serbia and the City of Belgrade, we are withdrawing our application and stepping aside at this time.' The Wall Street Journal, as relayed by BIRN, reported that Kushner gave up the plan after the indictment and due to the protests.

financial_stake.summary: A roughly $500 million hotel, apartment, office and retail complex that Kushner confirmed his company planned to finance, on a central Belgrade site Serbia leased for 99 years, which the draft agreement said could become free ownership. The project was withdrawn in December 2025, so no realized family profit is known.

title: Negotiates for the U.S. while owning Gulf-funded Affinity, with no confirmation or disclosure, CREW alleges

business_entity.name: Affinity Partners
business_entity.family_stake: Jared Kushner launched the investment firm A Fin Management LLC (Affinity Partners) after Trump's first term and is its sole owner, according to CREW's complaint citing Affinity's own SEC Form ADV filing.

government_nexus.action: President Trump named Kushner an "envoy of peace" on February 19, 2026, and Kushner negotiates directly with foreign leaders for the United States on the Israel-Hamas, Russia-Ukraine and U.S.-Iran conflicts and represents U.S. interests on the Board of Peace, without Senate confirmation or a public financial disclosure.

official.name: Jared Kushner
official.role: Presidential envoy for peace (unpaid; says he is a volunteer, not a government official)

also_officials.name: Donald Trump
also_officials.role: President (named Kushner an envoy for peace)

government_nexus.note: Affinity manages money for, and collects fees from, the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, all three of which sit on the Board of Peace, pledged at least $1 billion each to it, and were involved in the Israel-Hamas negotiations Kushner conducts; CREW says at least Qatar has also mediated U.S.-Iran talks. Fellow envoy Steve Witkoff, also unpaid but, AP notes, a formal government employee, filed the Ethics Act disclosure Kushner has not, so the public cannot check Kushner's assurances against his firm's Gulf clients. No court or ethics office has found that any diplomatic act benefited Affinity.

status: Lawsuit pending: CREW filed its complaint in D.C. federal court on October 14, 2026; no government answer or ruling yet. Kushner continues as envoy and has filed no public financial disclosure.
date_of_action: 2026-02-19 (Trump names Kushner an envoy for peace) through 2026-10-14 (CREW files suit)
what_changed: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and a senior White House adviser in Trump's first term, has represented the United States throughout much of the second term in talks over the wars between Israel and Hamas and between Russia and Ukraine, and in talks with Iran, working alongside Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. On February 19, 2026, Trump announced he was making Kushner a special envoy for peace. The next month the watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) wrote to the White House Counsel asking that Kushner's public financial disclosure report be collected within the 30 days the rules allow, noting that Witkoff had filed one as a special envoy. CREW says that when it asked the White House and State Department in July for any disclosures Kushner had filed, both said they had none. Kushner has said he is not "technically" a government official but "just a volunteer like other businessmen" who help when asked. At the same time he is the sole owner of Affinity Partners, an investment firm with more than $6 billion under management, about 99% of it from foreign investors including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates; Forbes estimated Affinity's management fees at about $60 million a year. All three countries sit on the Board of Peace, where Kushner represents U.S. interests. On October 14, 2026, CREW sued Kushner, Witkoff, Chief of Staff Susan Wiles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and several offices in federal court in Washington. **The complaint alleges Kushner "holds a continuing position and wields significant government authority without having been confirmed by the Senate and without having filed a single financial disclosure."** It asks the court to bar him from acting as an officer until he is confirmed and to order him to file disclosures; if the court finds he is not an officer, to order disclosures as a government official; and if it finds he is a private citizen, to bar him from exercising government power under the private nondelegation doctrine. Kushner has said he has "never taken a diplomatic action to benefit Affinity" and that his ethics counsel and the White House Counsel's Office confirmed he follows all applicable ethics rules.

financial_stake.summary: Kushner solely owns Affinity Partners, whose assets under management passed $6 billion by the end of 2025, about 99% from foreign investors including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE. Forbes put its management fees at about $60 million a year. Because Kushner has filed no disclosure for his envoy role, what he personally earns from Affinity is not public.

financial_stake.caveat: The asset, ownership and fee figures are CREW's, as cited in its complaint from Affinity's own SEC Form ADV filings, Bloomberg, Forbes and a 2024 letter from Sen. Ron Wyden; Kushner calls Wyden's $157 million fee estimate "false" but has not published another figure, and no filing shows his personal income from Affinity. Kushner says he has "never taken a diplomatic action to benefit Affinity, [him]self, or any investor," that Affinity's investors have never influenced his diplomatic positions, and that he "raised no additional funds for Affinity Partners since President Trump was elected to his second term." His attorney Chad Mizelle calls the suit "without merit," says CREW lacks standing, and says outside ethics counsel and government ethics attorneys "confirmed that his arrangements comply with applicable ethics requirements"; Kushner takes no salary and pays his own expenses. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly says his "personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements," and a White House official says there is nothing unusual about using a private envoy.

legal_context: CREW's complaint invokes the Appointments Clause (U.S. Const. art. II, sec. 2, cl. 2), which requires officers of the United States who hold a continuing position with significant authority to be appointed by the President with the Senate's advice and consent, and the Ethics in Government Act's public financial disclosure rules (5 U.S.C. secs. 13103-13105), which require covered executive-branch officers and employees, including special government employees above set pay levels, to file within 30 days of taking a position. In the alternative, if Kushner is a private citizen, CREW says his exercise of government power violates the private nondelegation doctrine. These are allegations in a pending civil suit; no court has ruled on them. Kushner and the White House say he is an unpaid volunteer to whom neither requirement applies; if a court agrees, his Gulf-funded business alongside his diplomacy would be lawful but concerning, not a violation.

Whether Kushner is an officer is CREW's allegation, untested in court. Disputed: Kushner, his attorney and the White House say he is an unpaid volunteer, not a government official, that his arrangements were reviewed and found compliant by ethics counsel, and that his business has nothing to do with his diplomacy; Kushner disputes Sen. Wyden's fee estimate. Re-verified 2026-10-17: the docket shows no government answer or ruling, and AP and NBC News reporting adds the responses of Kushner's attorney and the White House.

title: Reportedly pushed a $620M Pentagon loan to a startup that Trump Jr.'s firm had invested in

business_entity.name: 1789 Capital
business_entity.family_stake: Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at 1789 Capital, the venture firm he joined after his father was elected to a second term; the firm took a stake of undisclosed size in Vulcan Elements in its August 2025 $65 million funding round, according to ProPublica. Trump Jr. told the Financial Times, as quoted by House Natural Resources Democrats, that he was "very involved in the strategic decisions regarding where to invest our resources" at the firm; a 1789 spokesperson told ABC News that investment decisions are made by a three-person committee that does not include him.

government_nexus.action: On November 3, 2025, the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital announced a $700 million conditional loan commitment to Vulcan Elements and ReElement Technologies, of which $620 million is a direct loan to Vulcan, the largest in the office's history at the time; the same day the Commerce Department signed a non-binding letter of intent for $50 million in CHIPS Act incentives in exchange for $50 million of equity in Vulcan. ProPublica reports that the loan request was made by Peter Navarro.

official.name: Peter Navarro
official.role: White House Senior Counselor for Trade and Manufacturing

government_nexus.note: 1789 Capital invested in Vulcan about three months before the loan was announced. ProPublica, citing interviews and Defense Department records, reports that Navarro, a close friend of Trump Jr.'s, made the loan request; that Vulcan's was the only deal on the office's list initiated by a top aide to the President; and that staff were told it was a White House priority and finished it in weeks rather than the usual months. A week before the deal was announced, Trump Jr. hosted Navarro on his streaming show and urged viewers to buy Navarro's book. Estimates of Vulcan's valuation grew tenfold after the deal, a gain for its investors, including Trump Jr.'s firm. Nothing shows Trump Jr. asked for the loan, and he and 1789 Capital say they had no role in it.

status: Ongoing, not charged: lawmakers and an ethics group asked the Pentagon inspector general to investigate; no IG response or finding found, and DoD's one known reply to senators is not public. House Republicans blocked a subpoena of Trump Jr. in March 2026; Navarro calls the reporting fake news.
date_of_action: 2025-08 (1789 Capital invests in Vulcan Elements) through 2025-11-03 (Pentagon announces the $620 million loan commitment)
what_changed:
Vulcan Elements, a North Carolina rare-earth magnet startup launched in 2023, announced $65 million in new investment in August 2025. According to ProPublica, the investors included 1789 Capital, the venture firm Donald Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected to a second term; neither the firm nor Vulcan has disclosed the size of the stake. Trump Jr. told the Financial Times, as quoted by House Natural Resources Democrats, that he was "very involved in the strategic decisions regarding where to invest our resources" at the firm.

**Around September or October 2025, staff in the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital learned of a White House request to lend to Vulcan.** ProPublica reported in May 2026, citing interviews and Defense Department records, that the request was made by Peter Navarro, the President's senior counselor for trade and manufacturing and a friend of Trump Jr.'s. A Pentagon official who was not authorized to speak publicly said that of the dozens of companies the office was considering, Vulcan's was the only deal initiated by a top aide to the President. Another person involved in the deal said staff were asked to move at an unusually rapid pace and got the loan through in weeks: "The call came from the White House: We have to get this done." An official involved said such deals are generally vetted for many months, but this one was finished in weeks because staff were told it was a White House priority. It is unclear how the request was delivered or whether it was framed as an order or a recommendation. Navarro and Trump Jr. are close: Trump Jr. visited Navarro in prison, Navarro dedicated his latest book partly to him, and in October 2025, not long after word came down from Navarro to make the loan, Trump Jr. hosted Navarro on his streaming show and urged viewers to buy that book.

On November 3, 2025, the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital announced a $700 million conditional loan commitment (the Defense Department's own formal release followed on November 21) to Vulcan and its supply partner ReElement Technologies, of which $620 million is a direct loan to Vulcan, the largest in the office's history at the time. The same day the Commerce Department signed a non-binding letter of intent to provide $50 million in CHIPS Act incentives, in exchange for $50 million of equity in Vulcan. Estimates of Vulcan's valuation went from about $200 million near the time 1789 Capital invested to about $2 billion, ProPublica reported, citing Bloomberg; Warren's office says the loan was worth twice the company's entire valuation.

Congressional Democrats have pressed for answers. On January 22, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal and Andy Kim asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth how the Office of Strategic Capital decided to award Vulcan the loan, whether the process was competitive and how many companies competed; the Defense Department replied on March 10 in a letter that has not been made public, and Warren and Blumenthal said it failed to answer the vast majority of their questions. On March 25, 2026, House Natural Resources Democrats moved to subpoena Trump Jr., a Pentagon official and a Vulcan executive; the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee voted 5-2 along party lines to block it. After ProPublica's report, Warren, Blumenthal, Sen. Mazie Hirono and Reps. Jason Crow and Mike Levin wrote to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles asking whether Navarro acted at someone else's direction and whether the President knew; on June 3 the ethics group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington asked the White House Counsel's Office and the Defense Department's inspector general to investigate the loan; Sens. Adam Schiff, Warren and Blumenthal asked the Office of Strategic Capital on July 30, 2026 which White House officials contacted its staff about the deal; on August 4, Warren, Rep. Robert Garcia, Blumenthal and Sen. Tammy Duckworth asked the inspector general to investigate a reported $3.2 billion in awards to companies tied to the President's sons, naming the Vulcan loan first among the decisions of particular concern; and on August 11, 2026, Garcia and Rep. Jared Huffman demanded documents from Vulcan's CEO, John Maslin, saying the reporting contradicted his assurances of no political favoritism. No public answers to the later requests, and no inspector general response, were found. Navarro called the story "fake news on steroids." A White House spokesperson said the team, "including Senior Counselor Navarro," is working to secure the critical-mineral supply chain "at Trump Speed"; a Pentagon spokesperson said political connections "play absolutely no role"; and spokespeople for Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital said he never discussed Vulcan with Navarro and the firm played no role in the loan.

financial_stake.summary: 1789 Capital's stake in Vulcan is undisclosed, so the family firm's gain cannot be measured. On October 23, 2025, Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, who pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program, as part of Binance's $4.3 billion settlement with the Justice Department, and served four months in prison. **This pardon is the one tied to the Trump family's business: MGX, a state-owned Abu Dhabi firm, had paid for a $2 billion stake in Binance using USD1, the stablecoin of World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture co-founded by Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr.** The Wall Street Journal reported that Binance also helped build USD1's technology. title: Trump's sons back AI firms and data centers, and his accounts trade AI stocks, while he sets AI and chip-export policy

title: Trump's accounts trade thousands of stocks and bonds, including SpaceX debt bought two days before his launch policy

business_entity.name: Trump's revocable trust and personal investment accounts
business_entity.family_stake: Trump is the sole beneficiary of the revocable trust that holds much of his wealth; Donald Trump Jr. serves as trustee and holds sole voting power over certain assets, per an SEC filing (CNBC, July 29, 2026), and CNBC on August 13 called him the sole trustee. In May a White House spokesman told Fortune the assets are held in a trust managed by the president's children. The Trump Organization speaks for the portfolio and says outside institutions run it in fully discretionary accounts. Trump's 2025 disclosure lists eight investment accounts with at least $858 million in assets (CNBC).

government_nexus.action: Trump's official decisions touching companies and issuers his accounts hold: the August 20, 2026 National Space Transportation Policy, which directs agencies to expedite launch permitting and the Secretary of War and NASA to favor commercial launch services in a sector SpaceX dominates; a 2025 proclamation exempting dozens of coal plants, including all four Plant Bowen units, from stricter EPA toxic-air limits; a July 2025 executive order speeding data-center and power-infrastructure permitting; and the 2025 tax-and-spending law's Medicaid cuts affecting hospital bond issuers
government_nexus.note: Trump's accounts bought SpaceX shares in June and July 2026 and $1,000,001 to $5 million of SpaceX bonds on August 18, two days before he signed the space policy, and hold municipal bonds tied to a coal plant his proclamation exempted, a utility serving data-center demand and hospitals exposed to Medicaid cuts (Reuters, CNN, CNBC). The policies are his own acts; the holdings are his, in a trust his son oversees. Former Bush White House ethics lawyer Richard Painter told Fortune, "There's a financial conflict of interest if he has an ownership interest in the account. It doesn't matter who manages it," and asked, "If it's like a mutual fund, why not just buy a mutual fund?"; CNBC reported that investors seeking municipal exposure routinely use exchange-traded funds and other indexed products to avoid picking individual debt. Trump called Sen. Josh Hawley a "pawn" when Hawley's stock-trading ban would have reached the president, though not until 2029 (Fortune). No official body has found that Trump directed any trade or set any policy to benefit his holdings.

status: Ongoing: Trump's accounts keep trading, including SpaceX stock in June and July and up to $5 million of SpaceX bonds two days before his August launch policy, and hold municipal bonds CNBC put at up to $1 billion. No agency or court has found wrongdoing; the White House has not named his managers.
date_of_action: 2025 (Trump's accounts make more than 21,000 trades, by Bloomberg's count) through 2026-10-08 (disclosure of his August 2026 SpaceX bond purchase made public)
what_changed: President Trump returned to office without putting his investments in a blind trust, and his accounts have traded individual stocks in sums CBS News called unprecedented for a sitting president, including shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX, a federal contractor whose fortunes his administration's decisions can affect. Trump placed much of his wealth in a revocable trust bearing his own name with Donald Trump Jr. as sole trustee, an arrangement CNBC noted gives him more control than the blind trusts other recent presidents used. His annual financial disclosure showed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 by Bloomberg's count, which CNBC and Fortune also reported; Fortune valued them at between $600 million and $1.86 billion. A periodic transaction report he signed on May 8, 2026 listed, by CBS News' count, 3,642 transactions across 1,026 firms and funds between January 6 and March 30, 2026, worth between $212 million and $695 million in total. Fortune's review of that filing found the accounts sold big-tech stocks in the $5 million-$25 million range on February 10, the day after a chip-tariff carveout leaked; bought energy stocks in the weeks after the Iran war began, while Trump was downplaying the conflict; and bought shares of egg producer Cal-Maine during the egg shortage, selling them two months later for two to five times more. On August 12, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Robert Garcia, ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, sent Trump a letter listing 30 trades they called suspicious, among them $25 million in Meta stock sales days before a top adviser said the administration was serious about making data-center builders pay "all of the costs," and 29 trades in the private-prison companies GEO Group and CoreCivic, worth up to $990,000, in 2025 as those companies profited from his immigration crackdown. **They wrote that the trading raises questions about whether Trump is "using your knowledge of government activities, your official authority, or the vast megaphone provided by the Presidency to make investments or move markets to your personal benefit."** They asked him to name the managers who direct his trades and to answer by August 28. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told CNBC the lawmakers were recycling "the same, tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family, and his administration for a decade"; no answer naming the managers has been reported. SpaceX priced the largest U.S. initial public offering ever on June 12, 2026, at a $1.77 trillion valuation. According to Reuters, a disclosure Trump signed on August 12 and made public on August 22 shows he bought between $15,001 and $50,000 of SpaceX shares on June 23, among more than 1,000 stock trades that month. On August 20, Trump signed a new National Space Transportation Policy setting a goal of more than 1,000 U.S. launches and re-entries a year by 2030, directing agencies to expedite permitting and environmental reviews and the Secretary of War and NASA to favor commercial launch services; Reuters noted that the previous year's 178 launches were dominated by SpaceX. **A later disclosure, signed September 8 and posted by the Office of Government Ethics on September 22, shows Trump bought another $15,001 to $50,000 of SpaceX shares on July 10 and sold between $1,001 and $15,000 on July 17, a week in which SpaceX's share price fell 15%, Reuters reported.** Those trades were among 1,156 transactions he disclosed for July, worth between roughly $79 million and $270 million in total by CNBC's count; the largest were sales of $5 million to $25 million each of Microsoft and Amazon stock on July 20. Reuters described SpaceX as a U.S. military contractor that often seeks approvals from federal agencies, run by Trump's former adviser. Because the forms report only value ranges, they do not show the exact size of the SpaceX stake, or whether Trump still held SpaceX shares when he signed the space policy. A further disclosure, made public October 8, shows that on August 18, two days before Trump signed the space policy, his accounts bought between $1,000,001 and $5 million of senior unsecured SpaceX bonds paying 5.35% interest and maturing in July 2031, CNN reported; the purchase was among 517 trades that August, which also included purchases of up to $25 million of Meta shares and up to $6 million of Microsoft stock. The Washington Post reported that the bond buy differed from Trump's other recent disclosed transactions both in its scale and because most of his other purchases have been stocks, and that SpaceX sold bonds this summer to support its heavy spending on AI data centers. White House spokesman Davis Ingle repeated that the portfolio is "independently managed" through index-replicating model portfolios, but, the Post reported, did not answer who decided to buy the SpaceX debt or whether an algorithm executed the purchase. Some bond indexes include SpaceX debt, but a financial adviser who spoke to the Post on condition of anonymity said buying individual bonds to track a bond index would be unusual. "There is a conflict of interest. I'm not saying he's doing anything illegal, but this really gives the appearance of corruption," Richard Painter, the top ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, told CNN. Trump's accounts have also been buying bonds. Reuters reported in November 2025 that disclosures showed at least $82 million in corporate and municipal bond purchases from late August to early October 2025, most of them bonds issued by municipalities, states, counties, school districts and other entities with ties to public agencies. A CNBC analysis of his disclosures, published September 29, 2026, found that Trump ended 2025 with 807 municipal bond positions worth between $240.7 million and $797.6 million and has since disclosed at least 243 purchases in 2026 worth between $68.2 million and $233.8 million, for more than 1,000 positions worth between $300 million and $1 billion; unlike his stocks, the filings show the bonds being bought but not sold. "The scale of [Trump's] municipal bond exposure is unprecedented to my knowledge," Justin Marlowe, director of the Center for Municipal Finance at the University of Chicago, told CNBC. CNBC reported that some of the bonds are tied to issuers affected by his administration's actions: in February 2025 the accounts bought $50,001 to $100,000 of pollution-control bonds tied to Georgia Power's Plant Bowen, 57 days before Trump signed a proclamation exempting dozens of coal plants, including all four Bowen units, from stricter EPA limits on toxic air pollution, and afterward bought up to $200,000 more in debt tied to two other covered plants; four months after his July 2025 executive order to speed permitting for data centers and the power infrastructure they need, the accounts began buying bonds of the Omaha Public Power District, a utility whose demand growth S&P expects data centers to drive; and the accounts ended 2025 with 72 positions tied to hospitals and health systems, many of which depend on Medicaid spending the 2025 tax-and-spending law is projected to cut by about $900 billion over a decade, according to KFF, and kept buying hospital debt after the law was enacted. CNBC noted that some purchases do not point in his financial favor, such as Minnesota state debt bought 15 days after federal Medicaid officials deferred $259.5 million in payments to the state. Richard Painter, the chief White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, told CNBC, "President Trump's energy secretary wouldn't be allowed to hold this type of bond, in my opinion, but because presidents are exempt from typical conflict-of-interest laws, [Trump] has." CNBC found no evidence that Trump or his investment managers traded on advance knowledge of administration decisions, that his financial interests shaped those policies, or that he directed any transaction. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said neither Trump nor his family has "any ability to direct, influence, or provide input" on how the portfolio is invested, and a Trump Organization spokesperson said the outside managers have "sole and exclusive authority" over investment decisions. The White House says third-party financial institutions independently manage the portfolio through computer models that replicate "recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," and that neither Trump nor his family can direct when investments are bought or sold; Trump said in July, "They invest my money, and I don't talk to them." Presidents may legally trade securities as long as they report the trades, and the criminal conflict-of-interest statute that bars other executive-branch officials from working on matters affecting their own holdings (18 U.S.C. 208) does not cover the President or Vice President. Painter also told Fortune, "There's a financial conflict of interest if he has an ownership interest in the account. It doesn't matter who manages it," while declining to allege that anyone traded on government information, which he said disclosures cannot prove.

business_entity.family_stake: Donald Trump Jr. joined 1789 Capital as a partner days after the 2024 election and shares in its profit, The Washington Post reported, but does not sit on its investment committee, which a 1789 spokesperson told ABC News has three members. date_of_action: 2024-11 (Trump Jr. joins 1789 Capital days after the election) through 2026-10-06 (Trump announces Anduril shipyard and Navy deal worth up to $6.6 billion)
what_changed:
Within days of his father's November 2024 election, Donald Trump Jr. announced he was joining 1789 Capital, a Palm Beach, Florida venture firm controlled by Chris Buskirk and Omeed Malik, as a partner; since then the firm has gathered roughly $3 billion in capital under management, according to a person familiar with it. Eric Trump's main dealmaker is American Ventures, a branch of Dominari Holdings, a boutique investment bank located in Trump Tower, The Washington Post reported. Through these firms the brothers have backed companies that sell to the federal government. TAP tracks several individually: 1789 Capital invested in the rare-earth magnet maker Vulcan Elements months before the Pentagon committed a record $620 million loan to it; the Army and Air Force bought from the drone makers Unusual Machines and Powerus after the sons got involved; and the sons hold an indirect stake in Kaz Resources, a tungsten venture seeking federal financing.

Other companies in the portfolio have also won federal money. Foundation Future Industries, a humanoid-robot start-up where Eric Trump is chief strategy adviser, received $24 million in research contracts with the Army, Navy and Air Force in April 2026, according to lawmakers, though The Next Web reported that some were inherited through Foundation's acquisition of a company called Boardwalk, and WIRED reported that when it asked, the company shared two contracts inherited from Boardwalk and three that came through a Florida research institute, with no sign of new government money won on its own; on Fox Business on April 23, Eric Trump said "We are America First. We have to win this race." In March the Army awarded Hadrian, an AI-driven factory company backed by 1789 Capital, an initial $39.2 million and the Navy awarded it $900 million for automated submarine factories. PsiQuantum, a quantum-computing company that announced a 1789 Capital investment in September 2025, received a $100 million Commerce Department letter of intent in May 2026 and a $125 million DARPA agreement in July. On May 8, Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, told the Defense Department inspector general that companies tied to the Trump family "have amassed over $725 million in loans, grants, and awards since President Trump took office," and asked what contracts DoD has with Anduril, Foundation Future Industries and ten other companies.

**On July 13, 2026, The Washington Post reported that 15 companies backed by funds linked to the brothers had generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested**, plus $3.1 billion in future contract options, based on federal contracting databases, company announcements and PitchBook data. SpaceX and Anduril accounted for 97 percent of the direct cash; the 13 other start-ups had captured nearly $1.8 billion in long-term federal commitments and $103 million in direct cash after the brothers invested. Ten of the 15 had government business before the sons invested, and five got their first contracts afterward. The Post reported that Trump Jr. said at an investment conference that he "helped craft some of [the department's] messaging" and, on his podcast, that in helping Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth with personnel decisions he looked for candidates who wanted to spend more on drones. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said "There are no conflicts of interest"; a Pentagon spokesperson said "no company receives preferential treatment"; a 1789 Capital spokesman said "There are zero conflicts at 1789"; and Trump Jr. does not sit on the firm's investment committee, a person familiar with it said.

On July 30, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren wrote, citing recent reporting, that at least 14 companies working with the government on critical-mining deals have ties to the Trump or Lutnick families, with at least $8.9 billion in federal support provided or under consideration. On August 4, Warren, Garcia, Blumenthal and Sen. Tammy Duckworth asked the inspector general to determine which Pentagon awards since January 2025 involved companies affiliated with the Trump family and to review how they were decided, writing that they had "repeatedly sought, and failed to obtain" an explanation from the Pentagon and White House. A Trump Organization spokesperson said the brothers are "passive, minority investors" with "no role whatsoever in the awarding" of government contracts. In August, Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, wrote to 1789 Capital that it had "developed an uncanny ability to identify companies that are about to receive massive influxes of cash from the Trump Administration"; the firm's lawyers replied that "political association is not a substitute for evidence."

On October 6, 2026, President Trump appeared at Sparrows Point, Maryland, as Anduril unveiled a $3.7 billion shipyard to make Virginia-class submarine components; Anduril was also awarded a $2.9 billion Navy contract, and the two together are valued at up to $6.6 billion, Reuters reported. "American taxpayers will receive a 40% stake in the new shipyard," Trump said, without saying how. ABC News published an analysis the next day linking the deal to the sons, then removed it within a day, Mediaite reported, and on October 9 issued a corrected version saying the first "contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies." The corrected story says 1789 Capital invested $50 million in Anduril as part of a $2.5 billion funding round in 2025, a relatively small stake in a company valued at over $60 billion, and that a 1789 spokesperson said "Don Jr. has no ability to decide any investments at this fund." No public response from the inspector general has been found.

government_nexus.action: President Trump routinely uses Truth Social, Trump Media's platform, to announce or discuss decisions on tariffs, foreign affairs, energy policy and individual companies, Rep. Ritchie Torres wrote, and the press groups' lawsuit names White House aides Natalie Harp and Dan Scavino as officials who post his announcements there. Since August 1, 2026, Trump Media has sold paying firms machine-readable access to those posts milliseconds ahead of the platform's public feed.

also_officials.role: White House Deputy Chief of Staff

government_nexus.note: The family interest and the official act are the same posts: the President decides the timing and content of announcements that can move markets, and a company in which he is the largest shareholder, with about 41%, sells early, machine-readable access to them. Former White House chief ethics counsel Richard Painter argued the arrangement could violate federal law once Trump posts genuinely market-moving news, and former senior SEC official Renee Jones said material nonpublic information "belongs to the U.S. government or to the American people, not to Truth Social or President Trump." status: Pending: Judge Oetken heard the press groups' injunction bid against Truth API on October 7, 2026 and has not ruled; the government must respond to their complaint by October 30. date_of_action: 2026-08-01 (Trump Media launches Truth API early-access service) through 2026-08-12 (press groups sue to block it)
what_changed:
On August 1, 2026, **Trump Media & Technology Group launched "Truth API," a paid subscription service selling Wall Street firms machine-readable, accelerated access to posts from Truth Social's most-influential accounts -- including President Trump's own -- milliseconds ahead of the platform's ordinary public feed, priced at $60,000-$100,000 per month**; Fortune reported five subscribing firms as of early August 2026, which it estimated would bring in about $6 million a year, growing to "nearly a dozen" firms by mid-August. Trump owns approximately 41% of Trump Media (Nasdaq: DJT) and stands to profit from this recurring subscription revenue, even as he continues to use Truth Social routinely to announce or discuss tariffs, foreign-policy actions, and individual companies -- posts capable of moving securities and commodities markets. Legal and ethics experts identified this as a structural conflict distinct from ordinary data licensing: NYU economics professor Gian Luca Clementi called it "insider trading by definition"; Richard Painter, a former White House chief ethics counsel, warned it could violate federal law; and Renee Jones, a Boston College law professor and former senior SEC Division of Corporation Finance official, said "material nonpublic information belongs to the U.S. government or to the American people, not to Truth Social or President Trump." Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) sent a letter to SEC Chairman Paul Atkins around July 21, 2026 -- ahead of the product's launch -- asking the Commission to evaluate whether Truth API implicates federal securities law, market-manipulation protections, or broker-dealer obligations, and to coordinate with the CFTC and the Office of Government Ethics. Rep. Angie Craig wrote on July 21 to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and SEC Chairman Atkins demanding that the Justice Department and the SEC investigate Trump Media over what she called "the $100,000 per-month insider trading subscription service." On July 29, Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) announced their own letter to Atkins urging the SEC to investigate whether the arrangement violates federal securities law. Rep. Jamie Raskin, ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, separately launched an investigation on July 31, 2026, demanding records identifying the subscribing firms and the accounts available through the service. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer publicly called the arrangement "the definition of insider trading." On August 12, 2026, The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued President Trump in his official capacity, aides Natalie Harp and Dan Scavino, the Executive Office of the President, and the White House Office in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (The Intercept Media, Inc. v. Trump, before Judge J. Paul Oetken), represented by Yale Law School's Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic with co-counsel from Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, the Public Integrity Project, and Altshuler Berzon LLP. The suit alleges the arrangement violates the First and Fifth Amendments by giving unequal access to official government information to those who pay the President's private company. On August 31, the plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction that would bar the defendants from posting Trump's announcements on Truth Social while Truth API covers them, unless a free version is available at or before the same moment; the clinic's supervising attorney, Stacy Livingston, called Truth API "the work of a president who seems to be using his office to serve himself rather than the American people" and "anti-democratic and harmful to the free press." Two more suits followed. On September 17, the watchdog groups American Oversight and Campaign for Accountability sued Trump, Harp and others in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging that Truth API violates the First and Fifth Amendments and the Paperwork Reduction Act. On September 21, San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu sued Trump Media itself in San Francisco Superior Court under California's Unfair Competition Law, calling Truth API a "pay-to-play" scheme and asking the court to block it and impose penalties of up to $2,500 per violation; Trump is not a defendant in that case. Also on September 21, 53 former federal prosecutors and law enforcement agents who worked on public corruption and public integrity matters for the Justice Department -- among them Ty Cobb, a White House lawyer in Trump's first term -- filed an amicus brief backing the injunction, which Judge Oetken accepted. **The brief argues the scheme "poses an obvious risk of corruption" and could violate the Securities Exchange Act, the federal bans on illegal gratuities, conflicts of interest, and outside compensation for federal employment, and the Trade Secrets Act, potentially exposing both officials and paying subscribers who trade on early posts to criminal liability**; it expressly does not address whether those statutes reach the President or whether he could claim immunity. The government answered on September 24 that Truth API is a private Trump Media product rather than government action, that the President's posts reach the public in real time with a subscriber getting "at most" a 50-millisecond advantage, and that the amici's legal theories are "frivolous"; Trump Media filed its own amicus brief supporting the government, calling the plaintiffs' theory "wrong and frivolous." In their October 1 reply, the plaintiffs said more than a dozen subscribers were already paying up to $100,000 per month "for this supposedly negligible benefit." At the October 7 hearing, Judge Oetken called a 50-millisecond head start a "negligible delay to any human" but said subscribers' willingness to pay "suggests that whatever the time difference is, it's valuable," and asked whether Trump's ties to Trump Media were enough to justify an injunction against the White House; he did not rule from the bench and said he would issue a written decision later.

Update 2026-10-17: On October 13, Judge Oetken declined the government's request to put off its response to the complaint until he rules on the preliminary injunction, but extended its deadline from October 16 to October 30, 2026. The docket showed no injunction ruling as of October 17.

financial_stake.summary: Truth API costs subscribers $60,000 to $100,000 a month. Fortune estimated about $6 million a year in revenue at the five firms first reported, and up to $12 million a year at the more than 10 customers Trump Media announced in mid-August; by October 1 the press groups said more than a dozen subscribers were paying. The revenue goes to Trump Media, of which Trump owns about 41%; NPR wrote that "the Trump family's wealth will grow as customers sign up." The sums are small next to the company's reported $238 million loss for April through June 2026.

financial_stake.caveat: The revenue figures are Fortune's own arithmetic from the subscriber counts and list prices, not disclosed company results; Trump Media has not said which firms subscribe or what each pays, and Trump gains through his shareholding rather than a direct payment. Fortune notes that Truth Social posts are by design meant to become public within moments, "raising real doctrinal uncertainty" about whether faster access alone counts as insider trading. The subscriber counts come from Trump Media's own announcement and the plaintiffs' court filing. The government argues in court that Truth API is a private Trump Media data product, not government action, that the President's posts reach the public feed in real time and a subscriber gains "at most" about a 50-millisecond advantage, and that the amici's criminal-law theories are "frivolous." Trump Media, as amicus, calls selling faster machine-readable feeds ordinary industry practice and the plaintiffs' theory "wrong and frivolous"; its spokeswoman told NPR that Truth API offers "the fastest way to ingest publicly available Truth Social data" and called the senators' SEC letter partisan. Critics answer that subscribers would not pay up to $100,000 a month for a negligible edge, and Judge Oetken said at the October 7 hearing that the price "suggests that whatever the time difference is, it's valuable."

legal_context: Lawful-but-concerning as of now: no court, agency or congressional body has found Truth API unlawful, and no one has been charged. The pending S.D.N.Y. suit claims it violates the First and Fifth Amendments; the D.C. suit adds the Paperwork Reduction Act; San Francisco's state-court suit against Trump Media relies on California's Unfair Competition Law. Critics have pointed to insider-trading law under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78j(b), the misappropriation theory former SEC official Renee Jones described) and to the STOCK Act of 2012. The 53 former prosecutors' amicus brief argues the scheme could also implicate the illegal-gratuity statute (18 U.S.C. 201(c)), the conflict-of-interest and outside-compensation statutes (18 U.S.C. 208 and 209) and the Trade Secrets Act (18 U.S.C. 1905), but it expressly does not address whether those statutes reach the President or whether he could claim immunity. The government and Trump Media say the posts are public and no nonpublic information is sold.

title: Commerce eased UAE chip-export limits despite staff warnings; UAE-linked funds have deep Trump crypto ties

business_entity.name: World Liberty Financial
business_entity.family_stake: Per a May 2025 Senate Banking Committee minority release, Trump was listed as World Liberty's "Chief Crypto Advocate" and a Trump-affiliated entity controlled 60% of its ownership with a claim to 75% of its token revenues; by mid-2025 World Liberty's own disclosure said that entity, DT Marks DEFI LLC, owned about 40% of parent WLF Holdco and still received 75% of token-sale proceeds. Reps. Meeks and Kamlager-Dove say Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump co-founded it in 2024; Cointelegraph lists Trump and his sons Donald Jr., Eric and Barron among its nine founders. Eric Trump, as president of DT Marks SC LLC, a Trump family entity with an indirect stake in World Liberty's proposed trust bank, signed that entity's OCC passivity commitments.

government_nexus.action: On July 10, 2026, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security moved the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 to the more permissive Country Group A:5 and approved the UAE government and certain companies, including G42 and its subsidiary Core42, to receive advanced AI chips and servers license-free; the rule also says BIS will "favorably review" applications involving MGX semiconductors and servers bound for the UAE.

also_officials.name: Jeffrey Kessler
also_officials.role: Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security

government_nexus.note: The UAE beneficiaries are tied to World Liberty. Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE's national security adviser, chairs G42, and Sen. Warren calls him the royal "behind G42 and MGX." A Tahnoon-backed vehicle agreed four days before the January 2025 inauguration to buy 49% of World Liberty, directing $187 million to Trump family entities, and MGX settled its $2 billion Binance investment in World Liberty's USD1 stablecoin. Warren cites reports that Tahnoon later sought AI-chip approvals in meetings with U.S. officials, and Politico reports career Commerce staff had warned in fall 2025 that wider access for G42 risked diversion to China. Warren calls the rule a "corrupt deal"; no document or official finding ties the export decision to these investments.

status: Export-control easing remains in effect. Warren (Aug. 5) and House Foreign Affairs Democrats (Aug. 19, answers due Sept. 2) pressed Lutnick for the decision's rationale; no public Commerce or Treasury/CFIUS response has been identified.
what_changed: On February 13, 2026, Sens. Warren and Kim asked Treasury Secretary Bessent to determine whether CFIUS should formally review a UAE-backed investment vehicle's reported 49% stake in World Liberty Financial on national-security grounds, setting a March 5, 2026 deadline -- a request concerning the same underlying Trump-family/UAE financial relationship as the export-control decision described below, but made five months before it. No public Treasury response by that deadline has been identified. Five Senate Democrats (Warren, Blumenthal, Gary Peters, Durbin, and Wyden) then sent a June 23, 2026 follow-up letter escalating from a CFIUS-review request to a demand for public, sworn testimony from White House officials -- still short of a subpoena. On July 10, 2026, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced it was loosening export restrictions on sensitive technology to the United Arab Emirates, reclassifying the UAE into the more permissive Country Group A:5 and granting the UAE government and approved companies -- including G42, the UAE's state-backed AI company -- license-free access to advanced AI chips and servers, along with license-free eligibility for Commerce-controlled military items, certain commercial satellites and spacecraft, and dual-use items useful in civil nuclear power generation. **Politico reported that Commerce Department staff had compiled and circulated multiple internal reports and memos in fall 2025 documenting security risks tied to G42 and its affiliated companies, warning that eased restrictions could allow sensitive U.S. technology to reach China through Emirati intermediaries** -- one source telling Politico "it is an open secret that the UAE is the primary diversion point for sensitive U.S. technologies in the Middle East -- by orders of magnitude." Politico, citing three former officials and two other people familiar with the matter, reported that the administration "ignored warnings from career staff" in making the decision. The decision benefits a government with substantial, direct financial ties to Trump's personal business interests: Abu Dhabi-based investment fund MGX selected USD1 -- the stablecoin issued by World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture on which Trump is listed as "Chief Crypto Advocate" and in which, per a May 2025 Senate Banking Committee release, a Trump-affiliated entity controlled 60% of ownership (later cut to about 40%) and held a claim to 75% of token revenues -- to close a separate $2 billion investment into the crypto exchange Binance; separately, entities linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan -- the UAE's national security adviser, who chairs both G42 and MGX -- reportedly agreed shortly before Trump's January 2025 inauguration to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty Financial for $500 million. Sen. Elizabeth Warren publicly called the export-control easing a "corrupt deal," citing its promise of favorable treatment for MGX, the state-backed fund that had used Trump's own stablecoin for its $2 billion Binance investment; House investigators, led by Rep. Ro Khanna, separately opened a probe in February 2026 into World Liberty Financial's dealings with Abu Dhabi-connected entities, including whether $187 million flowed to Trump family entities. On August 5, 2026, Warren wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asking for the department's national-security analysis of the decision and whether the Defense, State, or Energy departments had raised concerns. Separately, the OCC granted World Liberty Trust Company preliminary conditional approval for a national trust bank charter on August 14, 2026, over public comments raising the same Trump-family/UAE conflict-of-interest concerns; the OCC called those concerns outside the scope of its review and obtained passivity commitments from certain World Liberty Financial investors rather than requiring divestment. On August 19, 2026, House Foreign Affairs ranking member Gregory Meeks and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove asked Lutnick whether he had discussed UAE export controls with World Liberty Financial representatives or Trump family members -- noting that BIS Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler had testified to the committee in July that he had not -- and requested answers by September 2, 2026.

financial_stake.summary: A Tahnoon-backed company agreed to buy 49% of World Liberty for $500 million, and $187 million of the first $250 million installment went to Trump family entities, per Wall Street Journal reporting. Sen. Warren, citing Trump's financial disclosure, says he made a $263 million windfall related to that deal. MGX's $2 billion Binance investment was settled in World Liberty's USD1 stablecoin, and a Tahnoon-backed company reportedly owns 49% of the parent of World Liberty's proposed trust bank, with a Trump family-affiliated entity owning another 38%.

financial_stake.caveat: The stake and payment figures are Wall Street Journal reporting relayed by senators, House Democrats and crypto outlets; the $263 million figure is Sen. Warren's reading of Trump's disclosure; the WLTC Holdings 49% rests on people familiar with the matter cited by the Journal and the family's 38% on one person. None of these figures measures a gain from the export decision itself. what_changed:

Elizabeth Warren and Chris Murphy wrote that Witkoff, as envoy, reportedly advocated for a previously stalled 2025 deal to export advanced AI chips to the UAE, and that around the time that deal was approved, a UAE government-backed firm invested $2 billion in WLF's stablecoin -- the Abu Dhabi fund MGX's use of WLF's USD1 stablecoin to close a $2 billion investment in the crypto exchange Binance, a separate, later transaction from Sheikh Tahnoon's January 2025 stake purchase. Update 2026-10-11: The New York Times reported on October 3, 2026, citing eight people familiar with the talks, that U.S.-Russia negotiations over ending the war in Ukraine had expanded to include a multibillion-dollar sale of the international oil fields, refineries and gas stations of Lukoil, the Russian oil company the Trump administration sanctioned in October 2025; Lukoil valued those assets at about $20 billion.
